1: What is that brahman? What is it that concerns the self? What is action, highest of persons? What is said to concern beings, and what is called that which concerns the gods?
2: Who is it that concerns sacrifice, and how is it here in this body, slayer of Madhu? And how are those who have control of themselves to know you at the time of departure?
3: Brahman is the imperishable, the highest. What concerns the self is called one's own nature. And the sending forth that brings the states of beings into existence is named action.
4: What concerns beings is perishable existence, and what concerns the gods is the person. What concerns sacrifice is I alone, here in the body, best of those who bear a body.
5: And whoever departs at the time of the end remembering me alone, letting go of the body, goes to my state of being. Of this there is no doubt.
6: Or again, whatever state of being one remembers when giving up the body at the end, that is the very state one goes to, son of Kuntī, having always been shaped into that state.
7: So remember me at all times, and fight. With your mind and buddhi fixed on me, you will come to me alone, without doubt.
8: With a mind yoked by the yoga of practice, a mind that goes to nothing else, one goes to the highest divine person, son of Pṛthā, by thinking on him.
9: A person may remember the seer, the ancient one, the ruler, who is smaller than the small, the supporter of all, whose form is beyond thought, who is the colour of the sun, beyond darkness.
10: At the time of departure, with an unmoving mind, yoked with devotion and with the strength of yoga, having rightly brought the breath to rest between the eyebrows, that person goes to that highest divine person.
11: There is that which knowers of the Vedas call the imperishable, which strivers whose passion is gone enter, and in desire for which they live the life of a student of brahman. That state I will describe to you in brief.
12: One restrains all the gates and confines the mind in the heart. One places one's own breath in the head and stays established in the holding of yoga.
13: Then, uttering Om, the brahman of one syllable, and remembering me, whoever departs, giving up the body, goes to the highest goal.
14: Whoever remembers me continually and always, with a mind on nothing else, is an ever-yoked yogī, and for that yogī I am easy to reach, son of Pṛthā.
15: Having come to me, those of great self, who have reached the highest perfection, do not meet rebirth, that home of suffering, which does not last.
16: The worlds, right up to the realm of Brahmā, return again, Arjuna. But for one who has come to me, son of Kuntī, there is no rebirth.
17: Those who know the day of Brahmā, which lasts a thousand ages, and his night, which ends after a thousand ages, are the people who know day and night.
18: When the day comes, all manifest things come forth from the unmanifest. When the night comes, they dissolve into that very same thing, which is named the unmanifest.
19: This very same multitude of beings comes to be again and again, and dissolves, with no will of its own, when the night comes, son of Pṛthā. When the day comes, it comes forth.
20: But higher than that unmanifest there is another existence, unmanifest and eternal, which does not perish when all beings are perishing.
21: It is called the unmanifest, the imperishable. They call it the highest goal. Those who reach it do not return. That is my highest abode.
22: But that highest person, son of Pṛthā, within whom beings stand and by whom all this is spread out, can be gained by devotion given to no other.
23: But I will tell you, bull of the Bharatas, the time at which yogīs who have departed go to non-return, and the time at which they go to return.
24: Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the sun's northern course: people who know brahman and depart then go to brahman.
25: Smoke, night, and likewise the dark fortnight, the six months of the sun's southern course: then the yogī reaches the light of the moon and returns.
26: For these two paths of the world, the bright and the dark, are held to be everlasting. By one, a person goes to non-return. By the other, a person returns again.
27: No yogī who knows these two paths is confused at all, son of Pṛthā. So at all times be yoked in yoga, Arjuna.
28: Whatever fruit of merit is declared in the Vedas, in sacrifices, in austerities and in gifts, the yogī who has known this goes beyond all of it, and reaches the highest place, the first.
